claim: Spontaneous DNA breaks instigate genomic changes that fuel cancer and evolution.
source: Spontaneous DNA breaks instigate genomic changes that fuel cancer and evolution, yet direct quantification of double-strand breaks (DSBs) has been limited.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws on established scientific knowledge about the role of DNA breaks in cancer and evolution.

claim: Direct quantification of double-strand breaks (DSBs) has been limited.
source: Spontaneous DNA breaks instigate genomic changes that fuel cancer and evolution, yet direct quantification of double-strand breaks (DSBs) has been limited.
evidence: This statement reflects the state of the field prior to this work, based on knowledge of existing methods.

claim: Predominant sources of spontaneous DSBs remain elusive.
source: Predominant sources of spontaneous DSBs remain elusive.
evidence: This statement characterizes the state of knowledge in the field before this study.

claim: GamGFP forms foci at chromosomal DSBs in Escherichia coli.
source: In Escherichia coli GamGFP forms foci at chromosomal DSBs and pinpoints their subgenomic locations.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures.

claim: GamGFP pinpoints subgenomic locations of DSBs in E. coli.
source: In Escherichia coli GamGFP forms foci at chromosomal DSBs and pinpoints their subgenomic locations.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3 using co-localization with TetR-mCherry markers.

claim: Spontaneous DSBs occur mostly one per cell in E. coli.
source: Spontaneous DSBs occur mostly one per cell, and correspond with generations, supporting replicative models for spontaneous breakage, and providing the first true breakage rates.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 2 and 4 showing the distribution of foci per cell.

claim: Spontaneous DSBs correspond with generations in E. coli.
source: Spontaneous DSBs occur mostly one per cell, and correspond with generations, supporting replicative models for spontaneous breakage, and providing the first true breakage rates.
evidence: This is demonstrated by microfluidic time-lapse experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: The correspondence of spontaneous DSBs with generations supports replicative models for spontaneous breakage.
source: Spontaneous DSBs occur mostly one per cell, and correspond with generations, supporting replicative models for spontaneous breakage, and providing the first true breakage rates.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observation that DSBs correlate with cell divisions.

claim: This study provides the first true breakage rates for spontaneous DSBs.
source: Spontaneous DSBs occur mostly one per cell, and correspond with generations, supporting replicative models for spontaneous breakage, and providing the first true breakage rates.
evidence: The study calculates rates of 0.021±0.008 DSBs per cell division from microfluidic data.

claim: GamGFP labels laser-induced DSBs in mammalian cells.
source: In mammalian cells GamGFP—labels laser-induced DSBs antagonized by end-binding protein Ku
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 5.

claim: Ku antagonizes GamGFP labeling of DSBs in mammalian cells.
source: In mammalian cells GamGFP—labels laser-induced DSBs antagonized by end-binding protein Ku
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B-D where Ku-deficient cells show better GamGFP recruitment.

claim: GamGFP co-localizes incompletely with DSB marker 53BP1.
source: co-localizes incompletely with DSB marker 53BP1 suggesting superior DSB-specificity
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figures 5 and 7 showing partial overlap of GamGFP and 53BP1 foci.

claim: Incomplete co-localization of GamGFP with 53BP1 suggests GamGFP has superior DSB-specificity.
source: co-localizes incompletely with DSB marker 53BP1 suggesting superior DSB-specificity
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that some 53BP1 foci lack GamGFP and vice versa.

claim: GamGFP blocks resection at DSBs in mammalian cells.
source: blocks resection
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6 showing reduced RAD51 foci in GamGFP-positive cells.

claim: APOBEC3A cytosine deaminase causes DNA breakage in mammalian cells.
source: demonstrates DNA breakage via APOBEC3A cytosine deaminase
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7 where APOBEC3A expression induces GamGFP foci.

claim: Some spontaneous DSBs occur outside of S phase in mammalian cells.
source: We demonstrate directly that some spontaneous DSBs occur outside of S phase.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 8 showing GamGFP foci in G1 cells.

claim: DSBs are the most genome-destabilizing DNA damage.
source: DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) are the most genome-destabilizing DNA damage (Jackson and Bartek, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Jackson and Bartek, 2009.

claim: DSBs promote deletions, genome rearrangements, chromosome loss, and point mutations.
source: DSBs (one- and two-ended) promote deletions, genome rearrangements (Hastings et al., 2009), chromosome loss (Paques and Haber, 1999), and point mutations (Harris et al., 1994; Rosenberg et al., 1994; Strathern et al., 1995).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: DSB-induced genomic instability promotes cancer.
source: DSB-induced genomic instability promotes cancer (Negrini et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Negrini et al., 2010.

claim: DSB-induced genomic instability promotes genetic diseases.
source: DSB-induced genomic instability promotes cancer (Negrini et al., 2010) and genetic diseases (O'Driscoll and Jeggo, 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citation to O'Driscoll and Jeggo, 2006.

claim: DSBs promote evolution of antibiotic resistance.
source: evolution of antibiotic resistance (Cirz et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cirz et al., 2005.

claim: DSBs promote evolution of pathogenic bacteria.
source: and of pathogenic bacteria (Prieto et al., 2006) including in biofilms (Boles and Singh, 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Prieto et al., 2006 and Boles and Singh, 2008.

claim: DSBs induce mutagenesis and genome rearrangement under stress in bacteria.
source: The latter reflect the role of DSBs in inducing mutagenesis and genome rearrangement under stress, which may accelerate evolution of bacteria (Al Mamun et al., 2012; Rosenberg et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Al Mamun et al., 2012 and Rosenberg et al., 2012.

claim: DSBs induce mutagenesis and genome rearrangement under stress in human cancer cells.
source: and human cancer cells (Bindra et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bindra et al., 2007.

claim: DSBs are implicated in mutation hotspots in cancer genomes.
source: DSBs are implicated in mutation hotspots in cancer genomes (Nik-Zainal et al., 2012; Roberts et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nik-Zainal et al., 2012 and Roberts et al., 2012.

claim: Neutral sucrose gradients do not routinely detect DSBs present in fewer than ~10% of a population of molecules.
source: DSBs have been quantified via neutral sucrose gradients (e.g., Bonura and Smith, 1977), or pulse-field gels (PFGE) (Michel et al., 1997), neither of which routinely detects DSBs present in fewer than ∼10% of a population of molecules, far above DSB levels that occur in cells spontaneously (Pennington and Rosenberg, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and describes limitations of existing methods.

claim: Pulse-field gels (PFGE) do not routinely detect DSBs present in fewer than ~10% of a population of molecules.
source: DSBs have been quantified via neutral sucrose gradients (e.g., Bonura and Smith, 1977), or pulse-field gels (PFGE) (Michel et al., 1997), neither of which routinely detects DSBs present in fewer than ∼10% of a population of molecules, far above DSB levels that occur in cells spontaneously (Pennington and Rosenberg, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and describes limitations of existing methods.

claim: The standard single-cell gel electrophoresis ('comet') assay detects single-strand DNA nicks and DSBs, and thus is not specific to DSBs.
source: The standard single-cell gel electrophoresis ('comet') assay (Olive et al., 1990) detects single-strand (ss) DNA nicks and DSBs, and thus is not specific to DSBs
evidence: This describes a limitation of the comet assay based on its mechanism and is supported by citation.

claim: The neutral comet assay is DSB-specific but lacks sensitivity.
source: whereas the neutral comet assay (Wojewodzka et al., 2002) is DSB-specific, but lacks sensitivity
evidence: This describes characteristics of the neutral comet assay supported by citation.

claim: The TUNEL assay detects free ends of DNA and nonspecifically labels both ssDNA nicks and DSBs.
source: The terminal transferase dUTP nick end-labeling (TUNEL) assay detects free ends of DNA, and so (nonspecifically) labels both ssDNA nicks and DSBs (Gavrieli et al., 1992).
evidence: This describes the TUNEL assay mechanism and limitation, supported by citation.

claim: γ-H2AX is a histone variant phosphorylated at sites of DNA damage during DNA damage signaling.
source: γ-H2AX is a histone variant phosphorylated at sites of DNA damage during DNA damage signaling.
evidence: This describes the nature of γ-H2AX based on established knowledge.

claim: γ-H2AX spreads over up to ~2-Mbp regions that comprise 500 to 8000 γ-H2AX molecules.
source: γ-H2AX spreads over up to ∼2-Mbp regions that comprise 500 to 8000 γ-H2AX molecules, so does not pinpoint DSB sites (Rogakou et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rogakou et al., 1999.

claim: γ-H2AX does not pinpoint DSB sites.
source: γ-H2AX spreads over up to ∼2-Mbp regions that comprise 500 to 8000 γ-H2AX molecules, so does not pinpoint DSB sites (Rogakou et al., 1999).
evidence: This is an inference from the spreading behavior of γ-H2AX, supported by citation.

claim: Numbers of γ-H2AX foci induced by DNA damage may not represent true numbers of DSBs.
source: Numbers of γ-H2AX foci induced by DNA damage may not represent true numbers of DSBs (Bouquet et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bouquet et al., 2006.

claim: γ-H2AX focus formation is variable and can occur at non-DSB sites.
source: and γ-H2AX focus formation is variable and can occur at non-DSB sites (Han et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Han et al., 2006.

claim: γ-H2AX may not always signify a physical break.
source: Thus, γ-H2AX may not always signify a physical break.
evidence: This is an inference from the previous statements about γ-H2AX limitations.

claim: 53BP1 is a non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) protein.
source: 53BP1 is a non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) protein
evidence: This is established knowledge about 53BP1 function.

claim: 53BP1 forms nuclear foci upon ionizing radiation (IR) treatment.
source: 53BP1 is a non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) protein and forms nuclear foci upon ionizing radiation (IR) treatment
evidence: This is established knowledge about 53BP1 behavior.

claim: 53BP1 focus formation depends on several histone modifications including γ-H2AX, H2A/X ubiquitylation and H4K20 methylation.
source: and forms nuclear foci upon ionizing radiation (IR) treatment, dependently on several histone modifications including γ-H2AX, H2A/X ubiquitylation and H4K20 methylation (Lukas et al., 2011b; Fradet-Turcotte et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lukas et al., 2011b and Fradet-Turcotte et al., 2013.

claim: The efficiency and DSB-specificity of 53BP1 are not known because histone modifications do not exist equally throughout the genome.
source: Because these histone modifications do not exist equally throughout the genome, the efficiency and DSB-specificity of 53BP1 are not known.
evidence: This is an inference from the dependence of 53BP1 on histone modifications.

claim: Ku is likely to be most specific for DSBs via its function in NHEJ.
source: Although Ku is likely to be most specific for DSBs via its function in NHEJ (Taccioli et al., 1994)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Taccioli et al., 1994 and knowledge of Ku function.

claim: Ku functions at telomeres.
source: Ku also functions at telomeres (Gravel et al., 1998)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gravel et al., 1998.

claim: Ku appears to interact with RNA polymerase II.
source: and appears to interact with RNA polymerase II (Dynan and Yoo, 1998)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dynan and Yoo, 1998.

claim: Ku binds ssDNA nicks, gaps, and regions of transition between single- and double-stranded structures.
source: Ku also binds ssDNA nicks, gaps, and regions of transition between single- and double-stranded structures, supporting concerns about its specificity (Paillard and Strauss, 1991; Blier et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Paillard and Strauss, 1991 and Blier et al., 1993.

claim: RecA binds ssDNA assisted by RecF.
source: In bacteria, RecA binds ssDNA assisted by RecF.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial DNA repair proteins.

claim: RecA is not specific for DSEs of DNA.
source: In bacteria, RecA binds ssDNA assisted by RecF. Neither is specific for DSEs of DNA.
evidence: This is an inference from RecA's binding to ssDNA rather than DSEs specifically.

claim: Bacterial Ku has been used to visualize DNA damage.
source: Bacterial Ku has also been used to visualize DNA damage (Kobayashi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kobayashi et al., 2008.

claim: Quantification of DSBs in living E. coli was achieved by measuring the RecB-dependent (DSB-specific) induction of the SOS response in individual cells by flow cytometry.
source: Quantification of DSBs in living E. coli was achieved by measuring the RecB-dependent (DSB-specific) induction of the SOS response in individual cells by flow cytometry (Pennington and Rosenberg, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pennington and Rosenberg, 2007.

claim: The SOS response assay could not determine the numbers of DSBs per cell.
source: Although this assay allowed quantification of rates of formation of living cells with DSBs (Pennington and Rosenberg, 2007), it could not determine the numbers of DSBs per cell.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the previous method.

claim: Precise rates of spontaneous DNA breakage in living cells are not known.
source: Thus, to date, neither precise rates of spontaneous DNA breakage in living cells nor the mechanisms that underlie most spontaneous DNA breakage are known, even in E. coli.
evidence: This characterizes the state of knowledge before this study.

claim: The mechanisms that underlie most spontaneous DNA breakage are not known, even in E. coli.
source: Thus, to date, neither precise rates of spontaneous DNA breakage in living cells nor the mechanisms that underlie most spontaneous DNA breakage are known, even in E. coli.
evidence: This characterizes the state of knowledge before this study.

claim: Replication-fork collapse at ssDNA nicks creates one-ended DSBs.
source: Replication-fork collapse at ssDNA nicks creates one-ended DSBs (Kuzminov, 2001)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kuzminov, 2001.

claim: Collisions of the replisome with transcription complexes cause DNA breakage.
source: Collisions of the replisome with transcription complexes (Merrikh et al., 2012) and other proteins (Gupta et al., 2013) cause DNA breakage.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Merrikh et al., 2012 and Gupta et al., 2013.

claim: Collisions of the replisome with other proteins cause DNA breakage.
source: Collisions of the replisome with transcription complexes (Merrikh et al., 2012) and other proteins (Gupta et al., 2013) cause DNA breakage.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gupta et al., 2013.

claim: In stationary-phase (non-replicating) cells, RNA/DNA hybrids left by transcription (R-loops) promote DNA breakage apparently by priming replication forks that then collapse at ssDNA nicks.
source: In stationary-phase (non-replicating) cells, RNA/DNA hybrids left by transcription (R-loops) promote DNA breakage apparently by priming replication forks that then collapse at ssDNA nicks (Wimberly et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wimberly et al., 2013.

claim: Spontaneous 53BP1 foci can be detected in G1 (non-replicating) human cells.
source: Similarly, spontaneous 53BP1 foci can be detected in G1 (non-replicating) human cells (Lukas et al., 2011a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lukas et al., 2011a.

claim: Most humans express up to nine primate-specific ssDNA deaminases: AID, APOBEC1, and seven distinct APOBEC3s.
source: Most humans express up to nine primate-specific ssDNA deaminases, AID, APOBEC1, and seven distinct APOBEC3s, all of which convert DNA cytosines to uracils (Conticello et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Conticello et al., 2007.

claim: AID, APOBEC1, and APOBEC3s convert DNA cytosines to uracils.
source: Most humans express up to nine primate-specific ssDNA deaminases, AID, APOBEC1, and seven distinct APOBEC3s, all of which convert DNA cytosines to uracils (Conticello et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Conticello et al., 2007.

claim: In humans, uracils in DNA can be processed by UNG2 into abasic sites and subsequently into ssDNA nicks by APEX.
source: In human, uracils in DNA can be processed by UNG2 into abasic sites and subsequently into ssDNA nicks by APEX.
evidence: This describes a known DNA repair pathway.

claim: DSBs have been inferred and associated with AID for Ig translocations in some B-cell cancers.
source: Although DSBs have been inferred and associated with AID for Ig translocations in some B-cell cancers (Robbiani and Nussenzweig, 2013), DSBs have yet to be identified directly.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Robbiani and Nussenzweig, 2013.

claim: DSBs have been inferred as intermediates in the generation of strand-biased cytosine mutation clusters in many cancers.
source: DSBs have also been inferred as intermediates in the generation of strand-biased cytosine mutation clusters in many cancers (Nik-Zainal et al., 2012; Roberts et al., 2012; Burns et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nik-Zainal et al., 2012, Roberts et al., 2012, and Burns et al., 2013b.

claim: Similar-sized mutation hotspots are targeted to DSBs created by I-SceI endonucleolytic cleavage in E. coli.
source: This inference is further supported by the demonstration of similar-sized mutation hotspots targeted to DSBs created by I-SceI endonucleolytic cleavage in E. coli (Shee et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shee et al., 2012.

claim: Similar mutation clustering occurs in yeast cells exposed to alkylating agents or engineered to express various human DNA deaminases.
source: and by similar mutation clustering in yeast cells exposed to alkylating agents or engineered to express various human DNA deaminases (Roberts et al., 2012; Taylor et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Roberts et al., 2012 and Taylor et al., 2013.

claim: Gam protein of phage Mu is highly DSE-specific.
source: We created fluorescent-protein fusions of the highly DSE-specific (Williams and Radding, 1981; Akroyd and Symonds, 1986; Abraham and Symonds, 1990) Gam protein of phage Mu
evidence: This is supported by citations to Williams and Radding, 1981, Akroyd and Symonds, 1986, and Abraham and Symonds, 1990.

claim: Gam is the ortholog of eukaryotic and bacterial Ku.
source: Gam is the ortholog of eukaryotic and bacterial Ku (d'Adda di Fagagna et al., 2003)
evidence: This is supported by citation to d'Adda di Fagagna et al., 2003.

claim: Unlike Ku proteins, Gam does not perform DNA repair reactions nor bind any other known protein.
source: but, unlike Ku proteins, does not perform DNA repair reactions nor bind any other known protein.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of Gam protein function.

claim: During phage infection, Gam binds and protects ends of linear phage DNA, preventing degradation by host exonucleases.
source: During phage infection, Gam binds and protects ends of linear phage DNA, preventing degradation by host exonucleases (Akroyd and Symonds, 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Akroyd and Symonds, 1986.

claim: Mu Gam is a highly specific DSE-binding protein biochemically.
source: Biochemically, Mu Gam is a highly specific DSE-binding protein (Williams and Radding, 1981; Abraham and Symonds, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Williams and Radding, 1981 and Abraham and Symonds, 1990.

claim: GamGFP detects about 71–82% of DSBs in E. coli.
source: GamGFP detects about 71–82% of DSBs, a robust efficiency.
evidence: This is calculated from experimental data comparing GamGFP foci to known DSB induction by gamma rays.

claim: A single GamGFP focus occurs per two-ended DSB in E. coli.
source: A single GamGFP focus occurs per two-ended DSB (Figures 2A–C and 3) or per one-ended DSB (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in the cited figures.

claim: A single GamGFP focus occurs per one-ended DSB in E. coli.
source: A single GamGFP focus occurs per two-ended DSB (Figures 2A–C and 3) or per one-ended DSB (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2E.

claim: GamGFP and GamEmGFP protein fusions produced in mammalian cells showed localization at laser-induced DSBs.
source: Similarly, GamGFP and GamEmGFP protein fusions produced in mammalian cells showed localization at laser-induced DSBs (Figure 5)
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: GamGFP was inhibited by Ku in mammalian cells.
source: were inhibited by Ku in those cells (Figure 5B–D)
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 5B-D.

claim: GamGFP inhibited resection at DSBs in mammalian cells.
source: and inhibited resection at DSBs (Figure 6)
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: GamGFPs validated indirect markers γ-H2AX and 53BP1 as genuine DSB markers by showing co-localization at laser and IR-induced DSBs.
source: For instance, GamGFPs allowed us to validate indirect markers γ-H2AX and 53BP1 as genuine DSB markers by showing co-localization at laser and IR-induced DSBs (Figures 5A,C,E–G, 7, 8)
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in the cited figures.

claim: 53BP1 foci in G1 contain DSBs.
source: Consistent with these results, we also demonstrate that 53BP1 foci in G1 contain DSBs that previously had been inferred only (Figure 8).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 8.

claim: There are DSBs identifiable with GamGFPs that are not seen with 53BP1.
source: Second, one aspect of the incomplete co-localization of 53BP1 with GamGFPs is that there are DSBs identifiable with GamGFPs that are not seen with 53BP1 (Figures 5G and 7C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figures 5G and 7C.

claim: GamGFPs may be more sensitive than 53BP1 to DSBs in Ku-defective MEFs.
source: One possible explanation is that, particularly in the Ku-defective MEFs (Figures 5G and 8), GamGFPs may be more sensitive than 53BP1 to DSBs
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation of GamGFP foci without 53BP1.

claim: In E. coli, GamGFP labels DSBs very rapidly, showing most foci by 10 min after phleomycin exposure.
source: At least in E. coli GamGFP labels DSBs very rapidly, showing most foci by 10 min after phleomycin exposure.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations described in the text.

claim: Some of the sites bound by 53BP1 may not possess frank DSEs.
source: Conversely, the presence of 53BP1 foci at sites that do not show GamGFP foci (Figures 5E–G, 7B,C), even in Ku80-deficient MEFs (Figure 5D), may indicate that some of the sites bound by 53BP1 may not possess frank DSEs, the Gam DNA substrate (Williams and Radding, 1981).
evidence: This is an inference from the incomplete co-localization data and knowledge of Gam substrate specificity.

claim: GamGFPs may be more selective and specific markers for DSBs than 53BP1.
source: With either possibility, the data suggest that GamGFPs may be more selective and specific markers for DSBs.
evidence: This is an inference from the co-localization data.

claim: APOBEC3A caused GamGFP foci in human cells.
source: Third, we demonstrate directly that primate-specific deaminase APOBEC3A caused GamGFP foci, and thus DSBs in human cells
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 7.

claim: DSBs result from DNA cytosine deamination in human cells.
source: indicating that DSBs result from DNA cytosine deamination.
evidence: This is an inference from the APOBEC3A experiment in Figure 7.

claim: Cytosine-deamination may be a general mechanism of DSB generation in mammalian cells.
source: Regardless of the specific mechanisms, the data indicate that cytosine-deamination may be a general mechanism of DSB generation in mammalian cells.
evidence: This is an inference from the APOBEC3A data.

claim: Cytosine deamination contributes a significant part of the cancer genome mutational landscape.
source: Cytosine deamination clearly contributes a significant part of the cancer genome mutational landscape (Nik-Zainal et al., 2012; Roberts et al., 2012; Taylor et al., 2013; Burns et al., 2013a, 2013b)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Spontaneous DNA breakage is precisely correlated with the number of cell divisions in E. coli.
source: In E. coli, GamGFP allowed demonstration that, first and importantly, spontaneous DNA breakage is precisely correlated with the number of cell divisions (Figure 4)
evidence: This is demonstrated by microfluidic time-lapse data in Figure 4.

claim: Most spontaneous breakage in E. coli results from DNA replication-based mechanisms.
source: providing the first evidence that most spontaneous breakage results from DNA replication-based mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference from the correlation of DSBs with cell divisions.

claim: Replication-fork collapse in engineered lambda phage produces DSBs.
source: These include fork collapse in engineered lambda phage (Kuzminov, 2001)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kuzminov, 2001.

claim: Fork-regression or 'chicken-foot' formation produces one-ended DSBs in cells with defective replication proteins.
source: fork-regression or 'chicken-foot' formation, to produce one-ended DSBs, in cells with defective replication proteins (Michel et al., 1997)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Michel et al., 1997.

claim: DSBs are created by collisions of replication forks with transcription complexes.
source: and DSBs created by collisions of replication forks with transcription complexes (Merrikh et al., 2012), and other proteins (Gupta et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Merrikh et al., 2012 and Gupta et al., 2013.

claim: The correspondence of spontaneous DSBs with the number of cell divisions implies that replication-based mechanisms are predominant causes of spontaneous DNA breakage normally in proliferating E. coli.
source: Our results demonstrate the correspondence of spontaneous DSBs with the number of cell divisions and imply that some or all of these mechanisms, and replication generally, are in fact predominant causes of spontaneous DNA breakage normally in proliferating E. coli.
evidence: This is an inference from the microfluidic data showing correlation with divisions.

claim: RNA (R-loop)-primed replication-fork collapse produces DSBs spontaneously in stationary-phase (non-proliferating) E. coli.
source: In separate work, we found that one particular replicative mechanism, in which RNA (R-loop)-primed replication-fork collapse produces DSBs, occurs spontaneously in stationary-phase (non-proliferating) E. coli (Wimberly et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wimberly et al., 2013.

claim: Most spontaneous DSBs result as single events per cell, not multi-break catastrophes in E. coli.
source: Second, the demonstration that spontaneous DSBs are generation dependent (Figure 4A), and our finding that most spontaneous DSBs result as single events per cell, not multi-break catastrophes (Figures 2C and 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in the cited figures.

claim: The rate of spontaneous DSBs is 0.021±0.008 per cell division in E. coli based on microfluidic data.
source: Our microfluidic data directly show rates of 0.021±0.008 spontaneous DSBs per cell division
evidence: This is calculated from microfluidic experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: The rate of spontaneous DSBs is roughly 0.011 per cell division in E. coli based on re-interpretation of previous data.
source: and the use of our data to re-interpret and correct previous indirect, low-resolution data (Pennington and Rosenberg, 2007) indicates a roughly similar rate of 0.011 spontaneous DSBs per cell division
evidence: This is calculated by re-interpreting previous data with new information from this study.

claim: True rates of spontaneous DSBs are 10–20-times lower than initial postulates.
source: These true rates are 10–20-times lower than initial postulates (Cox et al., 2000), but in line with each other.
evidence: This compares the calculated rates to previous estimates cited.

claim: Each DSB is 10–20 times more genome destabilizing than had initially been postulated.
source: Because genomic rearrangement frequencies remain the same regardless of estimations of DSB numbers, these rarer and more accurate break rates imply that each DSB is 10–20 times more genome destabilizing than had initially been postulated.
evidence: This is an inference from the lower DSB rates while maintaining the same genomic rearrangement frequencies.

claim: Chromosomally encoded Gam and GamGFP are functional in E. coli.

claim: RecBCD is a highly DSE-specific dsDNA exonuclease.
source: by demonstrating that their production blocks the action of RecBCD, a highly DSE-specific dsDNA exonuclease, in two assays.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RecBCD function.

claim: Lambda lacking its own Gam protein and Red recombination proteins forms small plaques because RecBCD DSE-dependent exonuclease prevents λ rolling-circle replication.
source: First, phage lambda (λ) lacking its own Gam protein (which, unlike Mu Gam, is a RecBCD-binding protein) and Red recombination proteins forms small plaques because RecBCD DSE-dependent exonuclease prevents λ rolling-circle replication (Smith, 1983) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Smith, 1983 and demonstrated in Figure 1C.

claim: λred− gam− forms large plaques on recB-defective E. coli because rolling-circle replication occurs.
source: By contrast, λred− gam− forms large plaques on recB- (or recC or recD)-defective E. coli because rolling-circle replication occurs (Smith, 1983) (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Smith, 1983 and demonstrated in Figure 1C,D.

claim: Wild-type E. coli producing either Mu Gam or GamGFP allow large plaque formation by λred− gam−, equivalent to those seen on recB-null-mutant E. coli.
source: We show that wild-type E. coli producing either Mu Gam or GamGFP allow large plaque formation by λred− gam−, equivalent to those seen on recB-null-mutant E. coli (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1D.

claim: Chromosomally encoded Mu Gam and GamGFP block RecBCD exonuclease activity.
source: We conclude that chromosomally encoded Mu Gam and GamGFP block RecBCD exonuclease activity
evidence: This is concluded from the lambda plaque assay results.

claim: Chromosomally encoded Mu Gam and GamGFP are functional for the Mu Gam DSE-binding activity.
source: implying that they are functional for the Mu Gam DSE-binding activity (Williams and Radding, 1981; Akroyd and Symonds, 1986; Abraham and Symonds, 1990).
evidence: This is an inference from the RecBCD blocking activity, supported by citations about Gam function.

claim: recB-null cells are highly sensitive to ultraviolet (UV) light because they are DSB-repair deficient.
source: Second, recB-null cells are highly sensitive to ultraviolet (UV) light (Willetts and Clark, 1969) because they are DSB-repair deficient
evidence: This is supported by citation to Willetts and Clark, 1969 and knowledge of RecB function.

claim: UV-induced damage can lead to DSBs.
source: and UV-induced damage can lead to DSBs (Bonura and Smith, 1975)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bonura and Smith, 1975.

claim: Induction of Gam or GamGFP in wild-type E. coli creates a phenocopy of the recB UV sensitivity that is almost identical to that of recB− cells.
source: We find that induction of Gam or GamGFP in wild-type E. coli creates a phenocopy of the recB UV sensitivity that is almost identical to that of recB− cells (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1F.

claim: Gam or GamGFP blocks RecBCD DSE-dependent exonuclease/DSB-repair activity.
source: These data, and those from the λ assay, show that Gam or GamGFP blocks RecBCD DSE-dependent exonuclease/DSB-repair activity
evidence: This is concluded from the UV sensitivity and lambda plaque assay data.

claim: Chromosomally produced GamGFP binds DSEs of DNA in living E. coli.
source: implying that chromosomally produced GamGFP binds DSEs of DNA in living E. coli.
evidence: This is an inference from the functional assays showing RecBCD blocking.

claim: Long-term Gam or GamGFP production confers poor viability, expected for DSB-repair-deficient cells.
source: Additionally, we also show that long-term Gam or GamGFP production confers poor viability, expected for DSB-repair-deficient cells, supporting a complete block to DSB repair (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: recBC null-mutant cells show severe loss of viability, with only about 30% of cells present in liquid cultures being viable and able to produce colonies.
source: recBC null-mutant cells show severe loss of viability, with only about 30% of cells present in liquid cultures being viable and able to produce colonies (e.g., Miranda and Kuzminov, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Miranda and Kuzminov, 2003.

claim: Long-term Gam production causes viability of 32 ± 9% viable cells relative to uninduced or WT cells.
source: In Figure 1—figure supplement 2, we show that long-term Gam production causes a similar low viability of 32 ± 9% viable cells relative to uninduced or wild type (WT) cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: GamGFP shows viability of 0.5% ± 0.06%, even though GFP production alone causes no reduction in viability.
source: GamGFP shows even further reduced viability (0.5% ± 0.06%), even though GFP production alone causes no reduction in viability.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: GamGFP is a better blocker of DSB repair than Gam.
source: the data imply that GamGFP is a better blocker of DSB repair than Gam
evidence: This is an inference from the lower viability with GamGFP compared to Gam.

claim: GamGFP blocks RecBC-dependent and also one or more RecBC-independent, residual DSB-repair pathways.
source: and that it blocks RecBC-dependent and also one or more RecBC-independent, residual DSB-repair pathways.
evidence: This is an inference from the lower viability of GamGFP producers compared to recBC mutants.

claim: When GamGFP is produced for 3 hr in cells without I-SceI endonuclease, spontaneous foci are visible in ~7.5% of cells.
source: First, when GamGFP is produced for 3 hr in cells without I-SceI endonuclease, spontaneous foci (presumably reflecting spontaneous DSBs, validated below) are visible in ∼7.5% of cells
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data described in the text.

claim: GamGFP forms foci in almost all cells when I-SceI is induced in cells carrying an I-SceI cutsite.
source: Second, GamGFP forms foci in almost all cells when I-SceI is induced in cells carrying an I-SceI cutsite (Figure 2B,C)
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2B,C.

claim: qPCR showed ~2–3 times more ori- than ter-proximal DNA copies under the experimental conditions.
source: qPCR showed ∼2–3 times more ori- than ter-proximal DNA copies under these conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The number of foci per cell is significantly greater when I-SceI cleavage is near ori than when it is near ter.
source: We find that although the number of cells with foci is the same with the I-site near ori as ter, the number of foci per cell is significantly greater when cleavage is near ori than when it is near ter (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2B,C.

claim: Cells with an ori-proximal I-site had 57 ± 2% of cells with >1 focus.
source: Whereas the cells with an ori-proximal I-site had 57 ± 2% of cells with >1 focus
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data quantified from Figure 2.

claim: Cells with a ter-proximal I-site had 14 ± 3% of cells with >1 focus.
source: those with the ter-proximal I-site had a significantly lower 14 ± 3% of cells with >1 focus (p=0.0001, Student's t test).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data quantified from Figure 2.

claim: Foci form proportionately to the number of DSBs per cell.
source: The data show that foci form proportionately to the number of DSBs per cell
evidence: This is concluded from the ori vs ter I-site experiment.

claim: Foci form at the DSB sites.
source: and imply that foci form at the DSB sites (supported independently below).
evidence: This is an inference from the proportionality of foci to DSBs.

claim: The two DSEs present in a single DSB appear to be kept close enough to each other that only a single focus is visible.
source: Rather the two DSEs present in a single DSB appear to be kept close enough to each other, either by GamGFP or perhaps by an E. coli DNA-repair or other protein(s), that only a single focus is visible.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation of single foci at two-ended DSBs.

claim: A TraI-dependent, four-fold increase in GamGFP foci occurs in F′-carrying cells compared with isogenic F− cells.
source: We observe a TraI-dependent, four-fold increase in GamGFP foci in F′-carrying cells compared with isogenic F− cells (Figure 2D,E)
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2D,E.

claim: GamGFP labels one-ended DSBs, in addition to two-ended DSBs.
source: implying that GamGFP also labels one-ended DSBs, in addition to two-ended DSBs such as those created by double-strand endonuclease I-SceI.
evidence: This is concluded from the TraI experiment showing foci at one-ended DSBs.

claim: Focus formation is linearly related to gamma-ray dose over the range of 0–140 Gy (r2 = 0.991).
source: We find that focus formation is linearly related to gamma-ray dose over the range of 0–140 Gy (r2 = 0.991) (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The efficiency of detection of DSBs as GamGFP foci is 71% based on comparison with sucrose sedimentation data.
source: Comparing this with the figure obtained by sucrose sedimentation of 0.031 DSBs/cell/Gy for E. coli (Bonura and Smith, 1977), we infer an efficiency of detection of DSBs as GamGFP foci of 71% (0.022/0.031 = 0.71).
evidence: This is calculated by comparing experimental data to published values from Bonura and Smith, 1977.

claim: Log-phase cells treated with bleomycin show significantly increased foci, with about 60% having one focus and ~34% having ≥2 foci.
source: We see that log-phase cells treated with bleomycin show significantly increased foci. About 60% have one focus and ∼34% have ≥2 foci (94% of cells with foci total), about 14-fold higher than spontaneous focus levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: GamGFP foci co-localize with the TetR-mCherry focus about 80% of the time with the I-site 10 kb from the array.
source: We find that GamGFP foci co-localize with the TetR-mCherry focus, producing a yellow focus, about 80% of the time with the I-site 10 kb from the array (Figure 3C,J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 3C,J.

claim: With 55 kb, 80 kb, and 2 Mb separating the I-site and tetO array, the mean distances between green and red foci increased to 0.45 μm, 0.52 μm, and to 0.57 μm respectively.
source: With 55 kb, 80 kb, and 2 Mb separating the I-site and tetO array, the mean distances between green and red foci increased to 0.45 μm, 0.52 μm, and to 0.57 μm respectively (Figure 3K)
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 3K.

claim: Sites farther than 80 kb apart are not necessarily further apart in space within the bacterial nucleoid after the nucleoid has suffered double-strand cleavage.
source: These data imply that sites farther than 80 kb apart are not necessarily further apart in space within the bacterial nucleoid (3-D chromosome structure), at least not after the nucleoid has suffered double-strand cleavage.
evidence: This is an inference from the interfocal distance data.

claim: GamGFP can diagnose subgenomic locations of DSBs.
source: These results indicate first, that GamGFP can diagnose subgenomic locations of DSBs.
evidence: This is concluded from the co-localization experiments in Figure 3.

claim: Beyond 80 kb, genomic locations are roughly the same physical distance apart in cleaved bacterial nucleoids.
source: Second, the data imply that beyond 80 kb, genomic locations are roughly the same physical distance apart in cleaved bacterial nucleoids (shown previously for sites >200 kb apart in uncleaved nucleoids [Wang and Sherratt, 2010]).
evidence: This is an inference from the interfocal distance data, supported by citation to Wang and Sherratt, 2010.

claim: GamGFP foci occur at DSB sites.
source: Third, the data support the conclusion (above) that GamGFP foci occur at DSB sites.
evidence: This is concluded from the co-localization experiments.

claim: Most spontaneous DSBs form with precise correlation to numbers of cell divisions in E. coli.
source: First, time-lapse microfluidic imaging shows that most spontaneous DSBs form with precise correlation to numbers of cell divisions
evidence: This is demonstrated by microfluidic time-lapse data in Figure 4.

claim: Most spontaneous DSBs form as 1 DSB per cell, not in multi-break catastrophes.
source: and as above (e.g., Figure 2A–C) they form mostly 1 DSB per cell, not in multi-break catastrophes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: Cells that were kept dividing in log-phase for 9 hr, then shifted to no-glucose for an additional 18 hr, show severely slowed divisions after the shift.
source: In Figure 4A, cells that were kept dividing in log-phase for 9 hr, then shifted to no-glucose for an additional 18 hr, show severely slowed divisions after the shift
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 4A.

claim: There is a highly precise correspondence of the numbers of spontaneous DSB foci with numbers of cell divisions at all division rates.
source: and a highly precise correspondence of the numbers of spontaneous DSB foci with numbers of cell divisions at all division rates (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: 45 ± 5% of cells formed GamGFP foci after phleomycin treatment at 27 hr in the microfluidic experiment.
source: To verify that the cells experiencing slow/no growth were still capable of forming GamGFP foci had breaks been present, we gave 20 μg/ml of DSB-producing agent phleomycin after 27 hr and found that 45 ± 5% (mean ± SEM) of cells then formed GamGFP foci (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, 32 hr).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Most spontaneous DSBs in E. coli form generation-dependently.
source: These results provide the first demonstration that most spontaneous DSBs in E. coli form generation-dependently
evidence: This is concluded from the microfluidic data showing correlation with divisions.

claim: The generation-dependence of spontaneous DSBs supports replicative models for the origins of most spontaneous DSBs.
source: and support replicative models for the origins of most spontaneous DSBs.
evidence: This is an inference from the generation-dependent formation of DSBs.

claim: The rate of formation of foci per division is 0.0145 ± 0.006 per cell division.
source: Figure 4A shows a constant frequency of cells with a single focus (mean 0.0145 ± 0.006 SEM per cell division; none had >1 focus) independently of cell-division rate.
evidence: This is calculated from microfluidic experimental data in Figure 4A.

claim: Correcting the rate of 0.0145 ± 0.006 foci per cell division for ~71% efficiency of detection provides a rate of 0.021 ± 0.008 DSBs per cell division.
source: Correcting this rate for ∼71% efficiency of detection of DSBs as foci (above), provides a rate of 0.021 ± 0.008 DSBs per cell division.
evidence: This is calculated by correcting the observed rate for detection efficiency.

claim: Under the same growth conditions (exponential growth in minimal glucose), 108 foci were observed in 98 cells with foci, or ~1.1 foci per focus-carrying cell.
source: We can correct this for the number of DSBs per cell by noting that under the same growth conditions (exponential growth in minimal glucose) we observed 108 foci in 98 cells with foci, or ∼1.1 foci per focus-carrying cell.
evidence: This is calculated from experimental observations.

claim: Applying the correction factor of 1.1 foci per focus-carrying cell to the previous estimate of 0.01 cells with ≥1 DSBs per generation gives 0.011 DSBs per cell division.
source: Applying this function to an estimate of 0.01 of cells producing ≥1 DSBs per generation (Pennington and Rosenberg, 2007), we have 0.01 × 108/98 = 0.011 DSBs per cell division.
evidence: This is calculated by re-interpreting previous data with the new correction factor.

claim: The rate of 0.011 DSBs per cell division is similar to the 0.021 ± 0.008 DSBs per cell division obtained from the microfluidic data.
source: This is similar to the 0.021 ± 0.008 DSBs per cell division obtained from the microfluidic data above
evidence: This compares two independently calculated rates.

claim: Both calculated rates are far lower than initial estimates.
source: and both are far lower than initial estimates (Cox et al., 2000), discussed below.
evidence: This compares the calculated rates to previous estimates cited.

claim: HeLa cells expressing GamGFP, in which DNA is sheared by a laser beam across the nucleus, display recruitment of fluorescence signal to the laser line.
source: We find that HeLa cells expressing GamGFP, in which DNA is sheared by a laser beam across the nucleus, display recruitment of fluorescence signal to the laser line (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: GamGFP co-localized with 53BP1 visualized by immunofluorescence staining in laser-treated and fixed samples.
source: GamGFP co-localized with 53BP1 visualized by immunofluorescence staining in the same laser-treated and fixed samples (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 5A.

claim: Less robust GamGFP localization at laser damage was observed in living than fixed HeLa cells.
source: We observed less robust GamGFP localization at laser damage in living (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) than fixed (Figure 5A) HeLa cells
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing data in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Pre-extraction of soluble GamGFP during fixation may increase the apparent signal from the bound GamGFP.
source: perhaps because pre-extraction of soluble GamGFP during fixation increases the apparent signal from the bound GamGFP (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism for better signal in fixed cells.

claim: ~Three-fold better labeling of laser-induced DSBs occurs in Ku-deficient cells compared with Ku-competent cells.
source: We found ∼three-fold better labeling of laser-induced DSBs in Ku-deficient cells (lacking Ku80, also known as Xrcc5−/−; in which Ku70 is also downregulated, Taccioli et al., 1994) compared with heterozygous Ku80-competent cells (Xrcc5+/−) or Lig4−/− (end-joining-defective but Ku-competent) mouse embryonic fibroblast cells (MEFs) (Figure 5B–D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 5B-D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Competition with Ku reduces GamGFP recruitment to DSBs independently of NHEJ.
source: Because GamGFP is inhibited by Ku even in end-joining-defective cells lacking LigIV (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), we infer that competition with Ku reduces GamGFP recruitment to DSBs independently of NHEJ
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that Ku inhibits GamGFP even in LigIV-deficient cells.

claim: γ-H2AX labeling of laser damage co-localizes with GamGFP.
source: We find that γ-H2AX labeling of laser damage co-localizes with GamGFP (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 5C.

claim: Only ~31% of foci per cell were coincident 53BP1 and GamGFP in Gamma-irradiated Ku80-deficient MEFs.
source: Interestingly, though both GamGFP and 53BP1 form foci on Gamma-irradiated Ku80-deficient MEFs, only ∼31% of foci per cell were coincident 53BP1 and GamGFP (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 5G.

claim: About 46% of foci showed only 53BP1 and ~23% showed only GamGFP in Gamma-irradiated Ku80-deficient MEFs.
source: About 46% showed only 53BP1 and ∼23% showed only GamGFP (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 5G.

claim: The coincident foci of GamGFP with γ-H2AX and 53BP1 validate both of these markers as genuine DSB markers.
source: The coincident foci of GamGFP with γ-H2AX (Figure 5C) and 53BP1 (Figure 5A,E–G) validate both of these markers, both indirect inferred DSB markers, as genuine DSB markers.
evidence: This is an inference from the co-localization data.

claim: Some of the sites that 53BP1 binds might not, at the moment of binding, possess a frank DSE because 46% are not bound simultaneously by GamGFP.
source: However, the data also imply that, as expected, some of the sites that 53BP1 binds might not, at the moment of binding, possess a frank DSE because 46% are not bound simultaneously by GamGFP (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is an inference from the incomplete co-localization data.

claim: Gam is specific for flush DSEs with up to a four-base single-strand DNA overhang.
source: This result is expected because, first, Gam is specific for flush DSEs with up to a four-base single-strand DNA overhang (Akroyd and Symonds, 1986)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Akroyd and Symonds, 1986.

claim: Gam does not bind the long single-strand DNA overhangs created by resection of DSBs by repair exonucleases.
source: not the long single-strand DNA overhangs created by resection of DSBs by repair exonucleases (Symington and Gautier, 2011).
evidence: This is an inference from Gam's substrate specificity, supported by citation to Symington and Gautier, 2011.

claim: 53BP1 is expected to have a post-DSB-repair presence because it binds modified nucleosomes rather than DNA.
source: Second, 53BP1 is expected to have a post-DSB-repair presence because it binds modified nucleosomes (Lukas et al., 2011b; Fradet-Turcotte et al., 2013) rather than DNA
evidence: This is an inference from 53BP1's binding mechanism, supported by citations.

claim: The ~23% of foci per cell with GamGFP alone indicates that some DSBs are present but not bound by sufficient 53BP1 to form a visible focus.
source: Similarly, the ∼23% of foci per cell with GamGFP alone indicates that some DSBs are present but not bound by sufficient 53BP1 to form a visible focus.
evidence: This is an inference from the incomplete co-localization data.

claim: In E. coli, GamGFP focus formation is very rapid, with 91 ± 0.5% of the foci resulting from a 10-min exposure to phleomycin appearing at 10 min.
source: At least in E. coli, GamGFP focus formation is very rapid, with 91 ± 0.5% (mean ± SEM, three independent experiments) of the foci resulting from a 10-min (pulse) exposure to 20 µg/ml phleomycin appearing at 10 min.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental observations.

claim: A more accurate picture of the locations of current DSBs containing frank DSEs might be obtained with GamGFP than 53BP1.
source: Whether because of timing, location or signaling, the data suggest that a more accurate picture of the locations of current DSBs containing frank DSEs might be obtained with GamGFP than 53BP1.
evidence: This is speculation based on the differences between GamGFP and 53BP1 labeling.

claim: Most of the cells that produced GamGFP had few (0–5) RAD51 foci.
source: Most of the cells that produced GamGFP had few (0–5) RAD51 foci, in optically sectioned nuclei in which all or most foci are expected to have been detected (Figure 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: Nuclei without GamGFP had increased RAD51 focus formation.
source: Those nuclei without GamGFP had increased RAD51 focus formation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: The data indicate exclusivity of the presence of GamGFP and resection.
source: These data indicate exclusivity of the presence of GamGFP and resection
evidence: This is an inference from the inverse correlation of GamGFP and RAD51 foci.

claim: GamGFP blocks exonuclease activity at DSEs in mammalian cells.
source: implying that as in E. coli (Figure 1C–F), GamGFP blocks exonuclease activity at DSEs in mammalian cells.
evidence: This is an inference from the RAD51 data and comparison to E. coli results.

claim: APOBEC3A is one of the most potent members of a family of DNA cytosine deaminase enzymes.
source: APOBEC3A is one of the most potent members of a family of DNA cytosine deaminase enzymes (Carpenter et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Carpenter et al., 2012.

claim: Induction of APOBEC3A or APOBEC3B results in both γ-H2AX and 53BP1 foci and frequent DNA breakage as determined by the comet assay.
source: Induction of APOBEC3A, or the related enzyme APOBEC3B, results in both γ-H2AX and 53BP1 foci and frequent DNA breakage as determined by the comet assay (Landry et al., 2011; Shinohara et al., 2012; Taylor et al., 2013; Burns et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: GamEmGFP forms foci in ~35% of cells when GamEmGFP and APOBEC3A are co-induced.
source: We find that GamEmGFP forms foci in ∼35% of cells when GamEmGFP and APOBEC3A are co-induced
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 7.

claim: Many of the GamEmGFP foci co-localize with 53BP1 when APOBEC3A is co-induced.
source: and many of the GamEmGFP foci co-localize with 53BP1 (Figure 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 7.

claim: The appearance of foci requires the catalytic glutamate of ABOBEC3A.
source: The appearance of foci requires the catalytic glutamate of ABOBEC3A
evidence: This is demonstrated by the catalytic mutant control in Figure 7.

claim: DNA cytosine deamination leads to DSBs in human cells.
source: strongly implying that DNA cytosine deamination leads to DSBs in human cells.
evidence: This is an inference from the APOBEC3A experiment requiring catalytic activity.

claim: Incomplete localization of 53BP1 with GamEmGFP implies that some 53BP1-bound sites may not have had Gam-recognizable DSBs.
source: As in MEFs (Figure 5), incomplete localization of 53BP1 with GamEmGFP (Figure 7) implies that some 53BP1-bound sites may not have had Gam-recognizable DSBs
evidence: This is an inference from the incomplete co-localization data.

claim: Some DSBs detectable by GamEmGFP did not possess sufficient 53BP1 to form a visible focus.
source: and some DSBs detectable by GamEmGFP did not possess sufficient 53BP1 to form a visible focus.
evidence: This is an inference from the incomplete co-localization data.

claim: Large 53BP1 foci in undamaged cells occur exclusively in G1.
source: The large foci in otherwise undamaged cells are only in G1, as shown by their CyclinA-negative state and tracking fluorescent 53BP1 throughout the cell cycle (Harrigan et al., 2011; Lukas et al., 2011a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Harrigan et al., 2011 and Lukas et al., 2011a.

claim: ~60% of the large 53BP1 foci in undamaged Ku80-deficient cells correspond to genuine GamGFP-detectable DSBs.
source: In this study, we examined the large nuclear 53BP1 foci in undamaged cells, previously shown to form exclusively in G1 (Harrigan et al., 2011; Lukas et al., 2011a), and find that ∼60% of the 53BP1 foci in Ku80-deficient cells correspond to genuine GamGFP-detectable DSBs (Figure 8).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 8.

claim: The GamGFP that coincides with 53BP1 foci contain multiple individual foci.
source: Moreover, the GamGFP that coincides with 53BP1 foci contain multiple individual foci
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 8.

claim: These DSBs may be in large multi-break clusters.
source: implying that these DSBs may be in large multi-break clusters.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation of multiple GamGFP foci within 53BP1 foci.

claim: GamGFP does not spread along DNA.
source: Because GamGFP does not spread along DNA, it can resolve multiple nearby DSBs
evidence: This is based on knowledge of GamGFP behavior from the study.

claim: GamGFP can resolve multiple nearby DSBs, which was not possible with 53BP1.
source: it can resolve multiple nearby DSBs, which was not possible with 53BP1 (Harrigan et al., 2011; Lukas et al., 2011a).
evidence: This is an inference from the properties of GamGFP vs 53BP1, supported by citations.

claim: Some spontaneous DSBs form outside of S phase, when most replication occurs.
source: These data indicate that some spontaneous DSBs form outside of S phase, when most replication occurs
evidence: This is concluded from the observation of DSBs in G1 cells.

claim: Some spontaneous DSBs form in clusters outside of S phase.
source: and do so in clusters.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation of multiple GamGFP foci in G1 53BP1 foci.
